usage: 빨갛다, a ㅎ-irregular, drops ㅎ before -아요
씻다 for water-washing, object particle 을
examples: 언니 얼굴이 정말 예뻐요.
My older sister's face is really pretty.
describing looks; possessive 언니 얼굴 needs no 의 in speech
저는 아침에 일어나서 얼굴을 씻어요.
I get up in the morning and wash my face.
note the verb 씻다, never 감다, takes the object 얼굴을
너무 부끄러워서 얼굴이 빨개졌어요.
I got so embarrassed that my face turned red.
빨개지다 = turn red; 이/가 marks the body part that changes
nuance: 얼굴 is the whole human face — both its looks and its surface you wash — and is the everyday word with no formality issue; you use it equally with friends and elders. Its near-synonym 낯 (as in 낯이 익다 'the face looks familiar', 낯설다 'unfamiliar') is old-fashioned and survives mostly in set idioms, so for plain 'face' always reach for 얼굴. Two pitfalls trip up English speakers. First, hair on the head is 감다 (감다 = wash hair) but the FACE is 씻다, the same verb as for hands and dishes — never say 얼굴을 감다. Second, English 'big face' does not transfer: a flattering 'small face' is 얼굴이 작다 (a real Korean compliment about proportion), and you do not say 얼굴이 커요 to mean handsome. Color uses 빨갛다 (얼굴이 빨개요), and to feel for fever Koreans touch the 이마, not the whole 얼굴.

Translating 'pretty face' as 얼굴이 이뻐다 with wrong spelling; the standard adjective is 예쁘다 → 예뻐요 (the ㅡ drops before -어요).
Using 얼굴이 커요 expecting it to sound flattering — in Korean a large face is unflattering; the compliment is 얼굴이 작다, 'small-faced'.

usage: 길다 describes length; 이 marks the subject
빠지다 = shed/fall out, intransitive, takes 이/가
examples: 제 머리카락이 너무 길어요.
My hair is too long.
describing length; 이 marks the strand as subject of 길다
요즘 머리카락이 많이 빠져요.
Lately a lot of my hair is falling out.
빠지다 is intransitive — the hair falls by itself, so use 이/가, not 을
미용실에서 머리카락을 짧게 잘랐어요.
I got my hair cut short at the salon.
자르다 takes the object 을; 짧게 'short' is the adverb form of 짧다
nuance: 머리카락 names the individual strands or the mass of hair as material, whereas 머리 is a slippery word that means both the head and, loosely, the hair growing on it. The dividing line: when you must be unambiguous that you mean the hair itself — counting it, shedding it, a strand on your food — choose 머리카락; for a haircut or hairstyle, casual 머리 is actually more common (머리 잘랐어 'I got a haircut'). One strand is 머리카락 한 올 (the counter 올 is for thread-like things). English speakers stumble two ways. First, English 'hair' is uncountable, but Korean lets you count strands, so 'a hair fell out' is 머리카락 한 올이 빠졌어요, not a plural. Second, hair falling out is 빠지다 (intransitive) — the hair leaves on its own — so it is 머리카락이 빠지다 with 이/가; learners wrongly force the object 을. And cutting is 자르다; 머리카락을 잘랐어요 means a trim, not amputation.

Mispronouncing/misspelling the verb as 자라요 (grow) when you mean 잘라요 (cut); 자르다 is a 르-irregular, so 'cut' becomes 잘라요.

usage: 넓다 'wide/broad', not 크다; 이 marks the subject
뜨겁다 ㅂ-irregular → 뜨거워요, a fever sign
짚다 = press-check for fever, object 를
examples: 제 이마가 좀 넓어요.
My forehead is a bit wide.
넓다 describes a broad surface — never 크다 for a forehead
열이 나서 이마가 뜨거워요.
I have a fever so my forehead is hot.
뜨겁다 → 뜨거워요 (ㅂ-irregular); 나다 collocates with 열 for 'a fever comes'
엄마가 제 이마를 짚어 보셨어요.
My mom felt my forehead to check.
짚다 is the precise verb for laying a hand to check temperature; 를 marks the spot
nuance: 이마 is the forehead, the flat span above the eyebrows, and culturally it is the spot Koreans touch first to check a fever — so it collocates constantly with 열이 나다 ('a fever comes') and 뜨겁다 ('hot'). Two register-neutral verbs matter: to lay a palm on it to gauge temperature is 짚다 (이마를 짚다), and a wide forehead is 이마가 넓다. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is dimension: a forehead has area, not bulk, so 'a big forehead' must be 이마가 넓다 ('wide'), never 이마가 커요 ('big'), which sounds odd and almost comical to Koreans. A second trap is the fever verb — English 'I have a fever' becomes 열이 나다 (literally 'heat comes out'), so you say 열이 나서 이마가 뜨거워요, not the direct 열을 가지다. Note 뜨겁다 is ㅂ-irregular, giving 뜨거워요, and to feel hot to the touch you generally use 뜨겁다 for objects/skin, while 덥다 is for the weather/air.

usage: 빨갛다 ㅎ-irregular → 빨개요; 이 marks the subject
뽀뽀하다 + location 에 for a peck
examples: 아기 볼이 통통해요.
The baby's cheeks are chubby.
통통하다 carries a warm, cute tone reserved for plumpness, not fat
밖이 추워서 볼이 빨개졌어요.
It was cold outside so my cheeks turned red.
빨개지다 'turn red'; cold weather reddens cheeks — a very common collocation
할머니가 손주 볼을 살짝 꼬집으셨어요.
Grandma gently pinched her grandchild's cheek.
꼬집다 = an affectionate pinch; 볼 (not 뺨) keeps it warm and loving
nuance: 볼 is the soft, fleshy cheek and carries an inherently warm, tender tone — it is the word for chubby baby cheeks (볼이 통통하다), cold-reddened cheeks (볼이 빨개지다), and affectionate pinches (볼을 꼬집다). Its near-synonym 뺨 also means cheek but anatomically/coldly and, crucially, collocates with violence: 뺨을 때리다 / 뺨을 맞다 is 'to slap / be slapped across the face'. So the dividing line is emotional temperature: 볼 is gentle and intimate, 뺨 is clinical or harsh. For everyday loving or descriptive talk always pick 볼. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 뺨 as a neutral dictionary 'cheek' and accidentally importing the slapping connotation; a sentence like 아기 뺨이 통통해요 sounds jarring because 뺨 clashes with the cuteness. Also note color is 빨갛다 (볼이 빨개요), the ㅎ-irregular dropping ㅎ before -아요, and a kiss on the cheek attaches with location 에: 볼에 뽀뽀하다.

usage: 아프다 for pain; 이 marks the body part
I rest my chin (on my hand)
my jaw came out of joint
examples: 오징어를 너무 씹어서 턱이 아파요.
I chewed squid too much so my jaw hurts.
아프다 → 아파요 (ㅡ drops); jaw pain from chewing is 턱이 아프다
손으로 턱을 괴고 멍하니 앉아 있었어요.
I sat blankly resting my chin on my hand.
괴다 takes the object 턱을; this is the set pose 턱을 괴다
저 모델은 턱이 뾰족해요.
That model has a pointy chin.
뾰족하다 describes a sharp V-line chin, a common beauty descriptor
nuance: 턱 covers both the chin (the point of the lower face) and the jaw (the hinge), and context alone tells them apart — there is no separate everyday word for each, so 턱이 아프다 from chewing means the JAW, while 턱이 뾰족하다 describes the CHIN's shape. Key collocations: resting your chin on your hand is the fixed phrase 턱을 괴다 (괴다 = to prop), a sharp chin is 턱이 뾰족하다, and a dislocated jaw is 턱이 빠지다 (where 빠지다 means 'slip out of joint', the same verb used playfully in 턱이 빠지게 웃다 'to laugh one's jaw off'). The English-speaker pitfall is expecting two distinct nouns and over-specifying — you do not need 'jawbone' vocabulary for daily life; 턱 does both jobs. A second trap is the verb for resting the chin: it is 괴다, not 놓다 or 대다, so 'I rest my chin on my hand' is 턱을 괴다. Note 아프다 is a ㅡ-stem (턱이 아파요), and the jaw 'coming out' uses intransitive 빠지다 with 이/가.

usage: 아프다 for pain, very common complaint
넓다 = broad; a physique compliment for men
examples: 오래 앉아 있어서 어깨가 아파요.
I sat for a long time so my shoulder hurts.
아프다 → 아파요; sitting too long is a classic cause of 어깨가 아프다
컴퓨터를 오래 해서 어깨가 너무 결려요.
I used the computer a long time so my shoulder is really stiff.
결리다 is the precise verb for a muscular crick — not 아프다 or 딱딱하다
엄마 어깨를 주물러 드렸어요.
I massaged my mom's shoulders (for her).
주무르다 → 주물러요 (르-irregular); -아/어 드리다 adds humble service to an elder
nuance: 어깨 is the shoulder, and the standout point is its dedicated stiffness verb 결리다: a tight, achy crick from posture or computer work is 어깨가 결리다, distinct from plain pain 어깨가 아프다 and never 어깨가 딱딱하다 (딱딱하다 = physically hard, used for objects). So learn the contrast 결리다 (muscle stiffness you feel) vs 아프다 (general pain) vs 딱딱하다 (hard to the touch). Broad shoulders, 어깨가 넓다, is a common physique compliment, and massaging them is 어깨를 주무르다 (주무르다 → 주물러요, a 르-irregular). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold. First, 'my shoulders are stiff' should not become 어깨가 딱딱해요, which describes a hard object, not a tired muscle — say 어깨가 결려요. Second, 어깨 also lives in idioms English can't decode literally: 어깨가 무겁다 'shoulders are heavy' = feeling burdened by responsibility, and 어깨가 으쓱하다 = feeling proud. Don't read those literally as physical sensations.

usage: 아프다 for pain; 이 marks the body part
들다 = lift up, object 을; ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ
I cross my arms / link arms
examples: 무거운 가방을 들어서 팔이 아파요.
I carried a heavy bag so my arm hurts.
아프다 → 아파요; the cause clause uses -아서 'because'
천천히 두 팔을 들어 보세요.
Please slowly raise both arms.
들다 takes the object 팔을; -아 보세요 = 'try ~ing' as a gentle instruction
친구랑 팔짱을 끼고 걸었어요.
I walked arm in arm with my friend.
팔짱(을) 끼다 is the set phrase for linking arms — not 팔을 끼다
nuance: 팔 is the whole arm, shoulder to wrist, and is most often the OBJECT of an action — you raise it, injure it, or link it. The verb to learn precisely is 들다 ('lift'): 팔을 들다 is the natural way to say 'raise your arm', and 들다 is a ㄹ-stem that drops its ㄹ before certain endings (들어요, 드세요). English speakers often substitute 올리다 ('raise/put up'), but 팔을 올리다 sounds slightly off for the natural gesture; reach for 팔을 들다. A second collocation worth memorizing is 팔짱(을) 끼다 — to cross your arms over your chest OR to link arms with someone, an idiom that does not break down word-for-word from English. Injuring the arm is 팔을 다치다 (다치다 = get hurt, takes 을), and arm pain is 팔이 아프다 with the subject particle because there 팔 is what hurts. Watch the particle flip: 팔이 아프다 (subject, it hurts) vs 팔을 들다 (object, you act on it).

usage: 아프다 for pain; 이 marks the body part
손가락 + instrumental 으로; 가리키다 = point at
examples: 문에 손가락이 끼어서 아파요.
My finger got caught in the door so it hurts.
끼다 'get caught/pinched'; 손가락이 (subject) is what hurts
칼에 손가락을 살짝 베었어요.
I lightly cut my finger on a knife.
베다 = a slicing cut; takes the object 손가락을 — not 자르다
피아니스트는 손가락이 길어요.
Pianists have long fingers.
길다 'long'; describing the finger's length with subject 이
nuance: 손가락 literally compounds 손 ('hand') + 가락 (a counter/word for slender stick-like things, as in 젓가락 'chopsticks', 가락국수 'thin noodles'), so it is transparently 'hand-stick' = finger. The crucial verb contrast is for cuts: a slicing wound from a knife or paper is 베다 (손가락을 베다), which means the skin is sliced, NOT 자르다. 자르다 means to cut something off, so 손가락을 잘랐어요 chillingly implies you severed the finger — a real and alarming mistake English speakers make because English 'cut my finger' uses one verb for both. Another trap is the toe: a toe is not a separate root but 발가락 (발 'foot' + 가락), so don't say 발 손가락. Pointing uses the instrumental: 손가락으로 가리키다. Finger pain where the finger is what hurts takes the subject particle (손가락이 아파요), while injuring it takes the object (손가락을 다치다). Note 아프다 and 베다 conjugate as 아파요 (ㅡ drops) and 베었어요.

손가락 literally compounds 손 ('hand') + 가락 (a counter/word for slender stick-like things, as in 젓가락 'chopsticks', 가락국수 'thin noodles'), so it is transparently 'hand-stick' = finger. A toe is not a separate root but 발가락 (발 'foot' + 가락).

The crucial verb contrast is for cuts: a slicing wound from a knife or paper is 베다 (손가락을 베다), which means the skin is sliced, NOT 자르다. 자르다 means to cut something off, so 손가락을 잘랐어요 chillingly implies you severed the finger — a real and alarming mistake English speakers make because English 'cut my finger' uses one verb for both. Another trap is the toe: don't say 발 손가락 — it is 발가락.

mistakes: Saying 손가락을 잘랐어요 to mean 'I cut my finger' — 자르다 means to cut OFF/sever; a slicing cut to the skin is 베다, so it is 손가락을 베었어요.
Inventing 발 손가락 for 'toe' — a toe has its own compound 발가락; 손가락 is strictly the finger.
Using the wrong particle when pointing: you point 손가락으로 (instrumental 으로), not 손가락을, so it is 손가락으로 가리켜요.

usage: 아프다 for pain, common in older people
꿇다 = kneel, object 을; only for kneeling
examples: 계단을 많이 올라서 무릎이 아파요.
I climbed a lot of stairs so my knee hurts.
아프다 → 아파요; stair-climbing straining the knee is a classic collocation
넘어져서 무릎을 다쳤어요.
I fell and hurt my knee.
다치다 takes the object 무릎을; -아서 links the cause 'fell'
무릎을 꿇고 진심으로 사과했어요.
I knelt down and apologized sincerely.
꿇다 is the dedicated verb for kneeling; 무릎을 꿇다 = to kneel
nuance: 무릎 is the knee, and 무릎이 아프다 is one of the most common aches, especially for older people and after stairs or squatting. The verb to lock in is 꿇다 — the dedicated word for kneeling, used only here: 무릎을 꿇다 means to drop to your knees, an act loaded with meaning (sincere apology, pleading, submission), so it is culturally weightier than English 'kneel'. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 앉다 ('sit') for kneeling — 무릎을 앉다 is simply wrong; kneeling has its own verb 꿇다. A second point: a swollen knee uses 붓다 ('to swell'), a ㅅ-irregular whose ㅅ drops in conjugation, giving past 부었어요 (무릎이 부었어요) — don't regularize it to 붓었어요. Injuring the knee is 무릎을 다치다 (object 을 because you act on/damage it), whereas the knee hurting takes the subject particle 무릎이 아프다. Note Koreans also say 무릎을 꿇리다 (causative) for forcing someone to kneel.

Conjugating 붓다 (swell) as 붓었어요; it is a ㅅ-irregular, so the past is 부었어요 (무릎이 부었어요).
Using the subject particle for injury: 'I hurt my knee' is 무릎을 다쳤어요 (object 을, you damaged it), not 무릎이 다쳤어요.

usage: 아프다 for pain; 이 marks the body part
긁다 = scratch an itch, object 을
examples: 딱딱한 바닥에 오래 누워서 등이 아파요.
I lay on a hard floor for a long time so my back hurts.
아프다 → 아파요; 등 here is the upper back, distinct from 허리
등이 가려워서 긁었어요.
My back was itchy so I scratched it.
긁다 = scratch; 가렵다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 가려워서 'because itchy'
엄마가 아기를 등에 업고 달랬어요.
Mom carried the baby on her back and soothed it.
업다 = piggyback-carry; the baby rides 등에 (location 에)
nuance: 등 is specifically the UPPER back — the broad surface from shoulders to mid-spine — and Korean sharply distinguishes it from 허리, the waist/lower back. This split matters because 'back pain' in English is one phrase, but Koreans pick 등이 아프다 for the upper back and 허리가 아프다 for the lower; most everyday backaches (from sitting, lifting) are actually 허리, so defaulting to 등 mislocates the pain. Key collocations: an itchy back is 등을 긁다 (긁다 = scratch), and 등을 돌리다 literally 'turn one's back' doubles as the figurative 'turn away from / betray', much like English. Carrying someone piggyback is 업다, with the rider on 등에. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 등 vs 허리 boundary — say 허리가 아파요 for lower-back/lumbar pain. Also note the itch adjective 가렵다 is ㅂ-irregular (가려워요), and 등이 아프다 takes the subject particle because the back is what hurts.

Reading 등을 돌리다 as only the physical act — it also carries the figurative sense 'to turn one's back on / abandon someone'.

usage: my chest hurts / my heart aches
뭉클하다 = a warm lump of emotion
examples: 계단을 뛰어 올라가서 가슴이 답답해요.
I ran up the stairs so my chest feels tight.
답답하다 here is physical breathlessness; 가슴이 marks the subject
좋아하는 사람을 보면 가슴이 두근거려요.
When I see the person I like, my heart flutters.
두근거리다 = heart-pounding from emotion; -면 'when/if'
그 영화의 마지막 장면이 너무 가슴이 아팠어요.
The last scene of that movie was so heartbreaking.
가슴이 아프다 here is EMOTIONAL pain, not physical — context decides
nuance: 가슴 means the chest physically, but it is also the seat of FEELINGS — Korean locates emotion in the 가슴 the way English uses 'heart'. So 가슴이 아프다 is a true double: it can be literal chest pain OR emotional heartache, and only context disambiguates (a movie scene → heartbreak; running stairs → physical). This is the central pitfall for English speakers, who assume body-part words stay literal: 가슴이 답답하다 may mean a physically tight chest or feeling emotionally stifled/frustrated, and 가슴이 두근거리다 is your heart fluttering from nerves or a crush, not a cardiac symptom. Distinguish the organ itself, 심장 ('heart' the pump, Sino-Korean 心臟), which is medical — 심장이 빨리 뛰어요 for an actual racing heartbeat — from 가슴, which is the emotional/anatomical chest. Useful collocations: 가슴이 뭉클하다 (touched, a warm lump in the chest), 가슴이 벅차다 (overwhelmed with emotion), 가슴을 펴다 (lit. open the chest = stand tall/be confident). Note 답답하다 and 아프다 are ㅡ/regular stems (답답해요, 아파요).

Reading 가슴이 답답하다 as only physical tightness — it commonly means feeling emotionally stifled or frustrated.

usage: 아프다 for pain, a top everyday complaint
가늘다 = slender; 이 marks the subject
굽히다 = bend the body forward, object 를
examples: 하루 종일 앉아 있어서 허리가 아파요.
I sat all day so my lower back hurts.
아프다 → 아파요; sitting long strains the 허리, not 등
무거운 상자를 들다가 허리를 삐끗했어요.
I tweaked my lower back while lifting a heavy box.
삐끗하다 = wrench/tweak; 허리를 takes the object as you injure it
허리를 쭉 펴고 바르게 앉으세요.
Straighten your back fully and sit up properly.
펴다 = unbend; 쭉 'fully/straight'; -(으)세요 polite command
nuance: 허리 spans both the waist (the narrow midsection) and the lower back/lumbar region, so 허리가 아프다 normally means LOWER-back pain — by far one of the most common complaints from sitting, lifting, or aging, and it is the word a doctor and a friend both use. This is the flip side of 등 (upper back): English lumps them as 'back', but Korean assigns lower pain to 허리 and upper to 등, so the key pitfall is saying 등이 아파요 for lumbar pain when you mean 허리가 아파요. On the waist side, 허리가 가늘다 ('slim waist') is a body descriptor, and clothing-wise your 허리 is the waistband measurement. Core posture verbs come in an opposing pair: 허리를 펴다 ('straighten/unbend the back', also figuratively 'stand tall after hardship') vs 허리를 굽히다 ('bend forward'); and a sudden tweak is 허리를 삐끗하다. Note 가늘다 is a ㄹ-stem (가늘어요) and 펴다 conjugates straightforwardly (펴요).
